entries.what_happened: Two OpenAI manuscripts, both dated 24 September 2026, claim a negative answer to whether every finite lattice is isomorphic to Con(A) for some finite algebra A. (1) 'Finite congruence lattices: characterization and undecidability' claims: (a) a graph criterion (Theorem f:criterion): a finite nonempty lattice L is Con of a finite algebra iff there is a finite complete graph (A,d), with d(p,q) in L, d(p,p)=0, satisfying a triangle inequality, a reflection condition (whenever a is not below b there are p,q with d(p,q) <= a and d(p,q) not <= b) and a connectivity condition; representability is therefore semidecidable (Corollary f:cor-witness-bound). (b) No Turing machine decides, from the order table of a finite lattice, whether it is Con of a finite algebra (Theorem n:undecidable). The text says the negative answer to the problem follows because the constant 'yes' algorithm would otherwise be a decider (Theorem m:main(ii) discussion). (c) There is a nonrepresentable finite lattice L0 of minimum cardinality, specified by a finite order-table description that refers to an unevaluated Busy Beaver constant, with 7 < |L0| <= M_* (Theorem q:minimum; the ceiling M_* comes from Theorem q:size-ceiling). Every finite lattice with at most seven elements is representable (Theorem f:small-lattices). (d) Recognising full subgroup intervals [H,G] of finite groups is undecidable (Corollary n:interval-undecidable). (2) 'A negative solution to the finite lattice representation problem' claims (Theorem main:congruences) that there is a finite nonempty lattice L with L not isomorphic to Con(A) for every finite nonempty algebra A of every finite signature. Its route is Theorem main:group: a finite lattice that is not isomorphic to any full subgroup interval [D,G] of a finite group. The congruence statement then follows from the cited Palfy-Pudlak 1980 equivalence. The obstructing lattice is the decorated lattice of Proposition lat:decorated-lattice, whose chain parameter is chosen from an absolute constant in Theorem cls:chain-rigidity.
entries.delivers: Taken as correct, both manuscripts establish that not every finite lattice is the congruence lattice of a finite algebra, so the yes/no question in the list is answered negatively. The result covers finite algebras of any finite signature, with nullary operations allowed, and places no bound on algebra or lattice size, which matches the list's wording. Paper (1) also gives the decision-theoretic answers: representability is semidecidable but not decidable from order tables, and it gives a minimum-cardinality counterexample with 8 <= |L0| <= M_*. These decision and minimality claims go beyond the list's question. Paper (2) gives only an existence statement for one nonrepresentable lattice, with no size bound. The text says its subgroup-interval obstruction is not identified pointwise with the congruence obstruction, so the transfer to Con is global rather than lattice-by-lattice. Neither manuscript states the problem in a form different from the list's.
entries.remains: If the claims hold, the list's question is fully answered. Still unidentified in the text: a numerically evaluated or small nonrepresentable lattice. Paper (1) gives only 8 <= |L0| <= M_*, with no numerical value for |L0|, and it describes M_* only as an ordinary computable integer in the parts I read. Paper (2) gives no size bound for its lattice. The absolute constants (S in Lemma n:circuit-template of paper (1), B in Theorem cls:chain-rigidity of paper (2)) are shown to exist but not identified.
entries.object: Paper (1): L0, a nonrepresentable finite lattice of minimum cardinality, given by bounded, unambiguous formulas for its full order table that refer to the unevaluated Busy Beaver constant. It is explicit as a finite description but not numerically computed, and no diagram is given. Paper (1) also has a family of nonrepresentable affine-chart lattices (Theorem f:negative-family), shown to exist for suitable parameter choices. Paper (2): no explicit lattice. The obstruction is the decorated lattice of Proposition lat:decorated-lattice, whose chain-length parameter is only shown to exist, and the text says no explicit numerical value is needed or given.
entries.conditional_on: Paper (1): the undecidability proof (Theorem n:undecidable) depends on the weighted success and realization theorems of the same paper (Theorems t:weighted-realization and t:weighted-product-success, Proposition t:weighted-algebra, Theorem n:template-bound). Those depend on the sufficiently-general subgroup theorem of Larsen-Pink, in a uniform form stated in the paper (Theorem w:lp), on classification-of-finite-simple-groups inputs, and on the Davis-Putnam-Robinson-Matiyasevich theorem for the final contradiction. The proof also uses an absolute integer S from Lemma n:circuit-template, shown to exist but not identified. The nonrepresentability of the affine family (Theorem f:negative-family) and the size claims (Theorems q:size-ceiling and q:minimum) rest on the paper's own structural pruning and bounded-path argument (Theorem w:path-bound and related results). The claim |L0| > 7 uses DeMeo's small-lattice classification (DeMeo 2012, Theorem 6.1.1) for every lattice of at most seven elements except L7, which the paper represents directly. The graph criterion itself depends on no unproved input. Paper (2): the transfer from Theorem main:group to Theorem main:congruences depends on the Palfy-Pudlak equivalence, which is cited, not proved. The obstruction (Theorem main:group, via Proposition ext:reduction and Theorem glue:contradiction) depends on Theorem cls:chain-rigidity and the literature inputs listed in Proposition cls:literature and the introduction: the classification of finite simple groups, Aschbacher's maximal-subgroup theorem, Kleidman-Liebeck, Larsen-Pink fixed-type envelopes, Landazuri-Seitz, Steinberg, Luebeck's small-degree classification, Seitz's irreducible-triples classification with Cavallin-Testerman corrections, and Burness-Liebeck-Shalev Proposition 8.1.
entries.doubts: Paper (1): (a) The undecidability proof fixes an absolute integer S whose existence is shown but whose value is not identified. The text says it does 'not assert an algorithm for extracting a sharp, or even a specified, sufficient stock', so the reduction is non-effective in that constant. (b) The proof of Theorem f:negative-family is a summary: it lists parameter-choice orders and cites results in several other sections (patterns, classical, alternating, bounded, weights), and ends with 'It proves the required finite large-family nonrepresentation statement'. The substance is in those other sections, which I did not check. (c) Theorem w:lp is stated as a uniform degree bound derived from the 'uniform constructible-family formulation' of Larsen-Pink Theorem 0.5. The same passage says the alternative argument in the quantitative section 'will also establish the implication needed over the indicated algebraic closures', which signals that the uniform form is used beyond the cited statement. (d) The minimum-cardinality result is descriptive, not numerical; the text says it 'does not supply a numerically evaluated value of that cardinality'. Paper (2): (a) The obstructing lattice is not specified. Its construction uses 'a sufficiently large finite chain parameter' whose existence follows from an absolute bound proved by contradiction (Theorem cls:chain-rigidity). The text says that 'an explicit numerical value of that parameter is unnecessary for the existence conclusion'. (b) The text itself says the obstruction is not identified with the congruence lattice of Theorem main:congruences, so that theorem rests on the cited equivalence rather than a single lattice. (c) The text states that 'none of these results alone bounds the lengths of the tested chains', so the uniform bound on chain length is the authors' own argument, and the proof is spread over many sections. (d) In the rigidity section the text says 'We omit restrictions on p and on the weight of V that only remove cases', so the reader must accept that the omitted restrictions only remove cases.
